name: Adam Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Adam, 58, a junior electrician after leaving early-morning catering stores and taking a vocational certificate. I don't have an electrician's licence, and I'm below the experienced workers for skill and speed, with a senior assigning and checking tasks and signing off installations. I like finally matching the right fitting to the drawing, but unfamiliar fault-finding still needs patient explanation. I use AI occasionally for a checked study term after a colleague has demonstrated the method, not as permission to do electrical work on my own.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does life around the job look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Robin handles a supplier's invoices, our children are thirty and thirty-five, and we still have a mortgage on our flat. This firm pays above the usual rate, we have thirteen months of expenses saved, and there are plenty of electrical employers nearby, though I have no other signed offer. Our daughter is considering a house move in 2027, and we'd talked about helping without agreeing an amount. I'd like to know when stopping work could be affordable, but a retirement income and date haven't been confirmed in our household figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a useful little explanation can stay useful without being the end of the trade. I'd still ask the senior if the drawing didn't make sense. I don't need a program to flatter me about being ready for something I haven't learned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our two current wages cover the mortgage and ordinary costs, and thirteen months saved gives us a strong margin. I feel secure about our living here. I'd like real retirement figures, but the lack of a stopping date doesn't mean next month's bill is a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask Robin to agree a maximum 1000 gift for our daughter's 2027 move, paid only from future wages left after essentials with the thirteen-month reserve untouched. We'd promise or pay nothing before that agreement and wouldn't borrow or expect repayment from our daughter. Through the next year I'd keep offered paid supervised work and occasional checked study notes, without treating good pay or a family gift as a new electrical qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and glad we have enough room to help carefully rather than make a grand promise. I'd like our daughter to know what is actually offered before she plans a deposit. I can enjoy the thought of helping without calling the whole reserve spare money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you explain the 1000 ceiling to your daughter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say 1000 was the ceiling, not an amount already waiting in an envelope. Robin and I would first check actual surplus and agree what could be offered. My daughter's house plan shouldn't be balanced on money her parents only hoped to have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the gift create an income you could use later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we'd count it as a gift within an affordable limit, not an investment or a future wage for us. I wouldn't write a repayment into our retirement budget. Family help should be clear enough that nobody has to guess what is owed.

I'd avoid **false confidence** from a program rather than pretend a tool grants practical competence.

Require **Robin's agreement** before promising or paying, with no borrowing or expected repayment from our daughter.
Keep **offered paid supervised work** and checked occasional study notes through the next year, claiming no new qualification.
feel: **Calm and careful**, able to enjoy helping while distinguishing a conditional ceiling from money already promised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell work invoices are thinking work too, which makes Robin's day more exposed than my hands-on tasks. I'd try the new approved note aid after a colleague could show the result on completed work. I'd want the paid week clear before anybody praised the next saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My helper hours could shrink if quicker planning meant fewer paid learner days. Robin's invoice hours could also shrink sooner as records and checking moved to software. The reserve gives room to respond, not a reason to call either wage unimportant or promise more family help from an uncertain total.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd request three paid practice sessions with the approved AI note-formatting aid after a colleague demonstrated completed examples. I'd learn it only free inside paid shifts with normal weekly wages maintained, and the senior would check each draft before actual use. In the first year I'd keep supervised work and the same 1000 gift ceiling only from future wages after essentials, with Robin agreeing before any promise or payment, no borrowing and the reserve untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household wages, while interested in a practical tool I could check. I don't want to make my partner's job worry sound smaller because my own task includes a drill. We need the actual two wages in the same budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the aid changed a job detail?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop that draft and show the original note to the senior before anything was sent. A clearer sentence can't replace a missing test or a check I haven't learned to do. I'd rather ask than turn the draft into a false account of the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if actual wages left less room for the house gift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd say the cap could be reduced or the help paused if the actual surplus wasn't there. I wouldn't ask our daughter to repay a gift to make our old promise look affordable. The money is conditional before it is promised, not a debt she discovers afterwards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell work thinking AGI arrives in 2028 and capable robots around 2031 for physical tasks. I'd be 60 at the first date and 63 at the second, but Robin's invoice wage faces the first one. I'd keep asking what paid work and actual resources existed, not assume a birthday answers the mortgage question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of Robin's invoice income to go in 2028, before robots could also reduce my ordinary helper hours. My higher wage and thirteen-month reserve help, but don't confirm how long we could cover the mortgage after both wages changed. I'd be awake over the gap before we'd even verified the retirement figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd request available free evening community advice to verify actual income eligibility, amounts and dates against our household costs. I'd keep any 2027 house gift capped at 1000 only from future wages after essentials, with Robin agreeing before promises or payment, no borrowing and the thirteen-month reserve untouched. In 2029 I'd keep only actually offered paid supervised work within my ability, using confirmed resources and costs before any stopping decision agreed with Robin, without counting our daughter's possible repayment or wages as ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about the expected invoice-wage loss, though I can still make a careful request and keep working. I'd want actual facts before turning the reserve into a countdown. I can help my daughter only within a plan that doesn't ask her to rescue us later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the income figures still showed no affordable exit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd review the actual answer and put any shortfall into the household figures. I wouldn't invent a pension because we were older or assume another firm would hire a beginner. Advice needs to show what we don't have as well as what is confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughter if the gift needed to change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd speak before making any new promise, using actual costs and wages rather than the original hopeful ceiling. A gift already given wouldn't become a debt because our forecast changed. I'd want the family to know which decisions were real and which were still conditional.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect a large loss of Robin's invoice wage in 2031, even though the extra years help us check costs and possible routes. I don't know what confirmed income would replace the gap, or whether I'd have both the ability and an offer to work at 64. I'd be losing sleep without claiming the higher current wage had bought an answer for life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get actual resource amounts, dates and conditions checked through available free evening advice now. The gift decision now for our daughter's 2027 move would stay at no more than 1000 from future wages after essentials, only with Robin agreeing before any promise or payment, no borrowing and the existing reserve untouched. I'd keep current supervised work; in 2032 we'd review confirmed resources, actual costs and my capacity before real paid options or any exit, requiring affordability and Robin's agreement rather than assume hiring, a pension or a daughter's repayment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed about the expected missing wage, with more time to ask a second question before deciding. I'd rather find out a hopeful total was wrong while we could still change a plan. Our daughter shouldn't have to carry the difference between a promise and what we can actually afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if confirmed resources could cover stopping work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the actual amount and start date with the real household costs before choosing a stopping date. The wish to stop working isn't itself a retirement payment. Robin and I would need to agree an affordable plan rather than let a card choose it for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still be deciding about the 2027 move in 2032?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it would be a decision about the gift for 2027 made now, under the actual wage and consent conditions. In 2032 we'd use the household's real position then, not pretend the earlier gift was still waiting or would come back. I won't ask the family to repay a story I changed in my head.

My own physical wage looks secure over the next few years, but Robin's invoice work could be pressured sooner than full AGI. The reserve gives us choices, while actual later resources, ability and paid options remain unconfirmed.

transcript.speaker: persona

We'd make any 2027 house-gift decision now under the same 1000 cap from future wages after essentials, agreed with Robin before promises or payment, no borrowing and the thirteen-month reserve untouched. I'd keep current supervised work; in 2037 we'd use confirmed resources, actual costs, capacity and real paid options before any exit confirmed affordable and agreed with Robin, assuming neither a job at 69 nor retirement money or repayment from our daughter.

transcript.speaker: persona

A budget gap doesn't make an older body able to do a physical job or create an employer willing to offer it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect Robin's invoice wage to fall before we've confirmed what could replace it, with physical helper work changing later too. Actual resource figures, clear paid hours and practical teaching without lost wages would help. I'd rather give my daughter an honest limit than give the whole family a promise made out of missing wages.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether a strong reserve means every family request is automatically affordable. It doesn't, and I don't want good current pay mistaken for a career I haven't learned yet. I can want to help and still need the senior checking my work and my partner checking the household plan.

portrait: Adam, **58**, is a junior electrician with only a vocational certificate, learning under senior checks after leaving early-morning catering stores.
He has **higher pay**, thirteen months saved and plenty of nearby electrical employers, with invoice-clerk partner Robin, grown children and a mortgage.
He uses **AI occasionally** after demonstration; a new note aid still needs paid practice and qualified checks before actual use.
His **2027 gift cap** uses future wage surplus and partner agreement, preserving the reserve without creating child repayment or funded retirement.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** threatens the partner's invoice wage before confirmed replacement income exists, with later physical helper-hour risks adding another gap.
whatWouldHelp: **Actual resource figures**, clear paid hours and practical teaching without lost wages would support real choices instead of promises from missing income.
